title: Record-Breaking Heat Wave Threatens Millions Ahead of July Fourth
summary: A brutal heat wave is set to shatter records across the Midwest and East Coast just as millions prepare for July Fourth celebrations. The National Weather Service (NWS) reports that more than 102 million people are under extreme heat warnings, with another 43 million under heat watches. Temperatures are expected to peak at 100 to 105 degrees Fahrenheit on Thursday and Friday, driven by a heat dome — a high-pressure system that acts like a lid, trapping hot air. NWS meteorologist Joe Wegman said the mid-Atlantic will see temperatures 10 to 15 degrees above normal. "We're expecting record-breaking temperatures," he said. The heat will be especially dangerous for older adults, those with respiratory issues, and pets, but Wegman stressed, "it's the kind of heat that affects everyone of all ages and health conditions." Humidity will make it feel even hotter, with heat indices reaching 105 to 115 degrees in parts of the Midwest and Mississippi Valley. Overnight lows will only drop into the 70s, offering little relief and increasing the risk of heat-related illnesses. Communities have opened cooling centers, and some summer camps and outdoor activities have been canceled. Scientists link the intensifying heat to climate change, primarily caused by burning fossil fuels. Ashley Ward, director of the Heat Policy Innovation Hub at Duke University, noted that the average number of heat waves in the U.S. has doubled since the 1980s. "The baseline is warmer," Ward said. "When a heat dome sets up, it's now starting from a hotter floor, making extreme heat more likely." Officials urge people to stay indoors, hydrate, and check on neighbors as the dangerous heat persists through the holiday weekend.
why_it_matters: As climate change makes extreme heat more common, today's teens will inherit a world where events like this aren't rare but routine—shaping where they can live, how they play, and what risks they face. Understanding the science and preparedness behind heat waves is essential for staying safe and advocating for a cooler, fairer future.

background_read: Heat waves are the deadliest weather-related events in the United States, killing more people on average than hurricanes or floods. This particular heat wave is especially dangerous because it coincides with the July Fourth holiday, when millions take part in outdoor activities like parades and fireworks. In 2021, a catastrophic heat dome over the Pacific Northwest shattered records and caused hundreds of deaths in the US and Canada, showing how quickly extreme heat can become lethal.

The National Weather Service (NWS, the federal agency that provides weather forecasts and warnings) issues heat watches and warnings to help communities prepare. A heat dome traps hot air like a lid on a pot, making the ground heat up day after day. The humidity makes it feel even hotter, and when night-time temperatures stay high, bodies don't get a chance to cool down, sharply increasing the risk of heat stroke.

Ashley Ward directs the Heat Policy Innovation Hub at Duke University (a research centre that studies how to protect communities from heat). Her finding that US heat waves have doubled since the 1980s reflects a global trend: as the average temperature rises due to greenhouse gases, heat extremes become more frequent and intense. The 'hotter floor' she describes means that even a normal weather pattern can produce record-smashing temperatures.

perspectives.description: Communities are responding proactively by opening cooling centres and cancelling risky outdoor events, showing that preparedness can save lives even during record-breaking heat. Advances in weather forecasting, like the NWS's early warnings, give people time to plan ahead and protect vulnerable neighbours.

Heat waves hit marginalised groups hardest—older adults, people without air conditioning, outdoor workers, and those with health conditions suffer disproportionately. The fact that overnight lows remain in the 70s means many cannot escape the stress, and the death toll from such events often only becomes clear weeks later, exposing inequalities in infrastructure and healthcare.

The data is clear: the average number of US heat waves has doubled since the 1980s, and the baseline temperature is rising. This isn't just a one-off weather freak but part of a long-term trend linked to burning fossil fuels. Scientists use heat indices and historical records to show that a warmer climate makes extreme events more likely, turning everyday heat domes into life-threatening emergencies.

If warming continues, heat waves like this could become the new normal by mid-century. That might force cities to rethink design—planting more trees, creating cool pavements, and mandating air conditioning in new homes. Youth activism and voting will play a key role in deciding whether countries accelerate the switch away from fossil fuels, directly shaping how hot summers will get in their own lifetimes.
